newsitem.title: CANADA: GOLF-DUNLAP EXTENDS LEAD AT CANADIAN OPEN.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-DUNLAP EXTENDS LEAD AT CANADIAN OPEN.

text.p: Unheralded Scott Dunlap, feeling at home north of the border, plundered the long holes again to extend his lead to three strokes after the second round at the Bell Canadian Open on Friday.
Dunlap recovered from a bogey at the first hole to card a seven-under-par 65 in a testing breeze at Glen Abbey.
He posted a 15-under 129 halfway total, the lowest in the 19 years the event has been held at the Jack Nicklaus-designed course in the Toronto suburbs.
He was three strokes ahead of fellow American Dudley Hart (64), while David Duval (65), Michael Bradley (64) and Taylor Smith (66) were five shots back.
Tiger Woods, the three-time U.S. amateur champion, made the cut again as he did in his pro debut in Milwaukee last week, but was 11 shots off the pace after a second straight 70.
Dunlap, a 33-year-old in his rookie season on the PGA Tour, eagled two of the par-fives and birdied the other two. Through 36 holes, he was an impressive 11 under on the par-fives.
"You can do some damage on the par fives if you drive the ball in the fairway," said Dunlap, who ranks only 88th in driving distance on tour this year.

Canada seems to agree with Dunlap. He won twice on the Canadian Tour before finally earning his PGA Tour card last year on his ninth try, and he finished eighth at last year's Canadian Open, his best result on tour.
However, he has hardly set the world on fire this year, and is a lowly 192nd on the money list.
"I'm used to choking on the cut," said Dunlap, unaccustomed as he is to leading. "It's nice not to have to worry about it for a change. There wasn't anything to choke on today.
"I couldn't believe today's round was as good as yesterday's. It would be insane to think I can maintain this place. It's hard to have confidence when your two previous years have been rubbish."
Meanwhile, Hart's 64 was the day's equal lowest round, and it was a welcome tonic as he battles back from injury.
In June last year, he tore ligaments in his right wrist hitting a tree root, and surgery last December kept him out of the game until June this year.
"When I came back I was ready to play, excited about the game again," he said.
The cut fell at even-par 144. Among those to miss it were U.S. Open champion Steve Jones, U.S. Ryder Cup captain Tom Kite and last year's British Open champion John Daly.
